screens.title: State and Chain of Responsibility Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore two behavioral patterns that tame conditional complexity. First, you will learn the State pattern, which models behavior variations by encapsulating each state into its own class so an object effectively changes its behavior as its internal state changes. You will see how a MediaPlayer can move between Playing, Paused, and Stopped without sprawling switch statements. Second, you will learn the Chain of Responsibility pattern, which lets a request travel through a sequence of handlers until one handles it, useful for logging levels, approval flows, or multi-stage processing. We will walk through Java examples for both patterns, point out common pitfalls such as mutable shared state or chains that never terminate, and practice a small approval workflow. By the end you will know how to choose between encapsulating state transitions or delegating handling in a chain, how to implement each pattern in Java, and where each pattern improves maintainability. Think about how these patterns reduce coupling and make behavior easier to extend.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › State & Chain Patterns
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

State and Chain of Responsibility Patterns

Learn how to remove complex conditional logic by encapsulating state-dependent behavior, and how to build flexible processing pipelines that pass requests along a configurable chain of handlers. Real Java examples demonstrate these ideas.

Concept Preview
State: MediaPlayer
Each state class defines play, pause, stop behavior. Context delegates.
Chain: Logger/Approvals
Requests traverse a chain; handlers decide to handle or pass on.
In this lesson
State pattern animation
Visualize transitions for MediaPlayer states and actions.
Java live coding
Implement PlayerState, concrete states, and MediaPlayer context.
Chain demo & activity
Logger chain and approval workflow exercise in Java.
Coming up
Key Outcome

You will be able to pick and implement the pattern that reduces conditional complexity and improves extensibility in your Java designs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1

That means you will be able to describe how a context delegates to state objects and why this keeps conditional logic out of the context. Second, you will implement the State pattern in Java: write a state interface, concrete state classes, and a context such as a MediaPlayer that switches states. You will practice a concrete example where play, pause, and stop are delegated to state objects. Third, you will understand the Chain of Responsibility pattern, how it decouples senders from receivers and how a request flows along handlers. Fourth, you will apply Chain of Responsibility to build flexible pipelines like logging or approval flows where each handler decides to handle or pass the request. Each objective includes a short cognitive goal and a practical reason why it matters, so you can connect the concept to real design choices.

screens.title: What is the State pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: The State pattern is a behavioral design pattern that lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes. In plain terms, instead of a single class filled with if-else or switch blocks checking a state variable, you model each distinct state as a class that implements a common state interface. The original object, called the context, holds a reference to the current state and delegates state-specific operations to it. A concrete example from the source is a MediaPlayer: Playing, Paused, and Stopped are separate classes implementing play, pause, and stop methods. When the context delegates a call to its current state, the result depends on that state’s implementation. This makes adding a new state a matter of adding a new class rather than modifying a large conditional. A common misconception is to think you should share a single mutable state instance between contexts to save objects. That often leads to subtle bugs: prefer distinct state instances or manage shared instances carefully. In short, State trades conditional complexity for small, focused classes and clearer transition logic. Consider: what state transitions in your app are causing long conditional chains?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › State Pattern
Core Concept

State pattern overview

Encapsulate varying behavior in separate state classes and let context delegate requests to the current state object.

When to prefer
When behavior branches heavily on an internal state and new states may be added over time.
Common pitfalls
  • Sharing mutable state instances across contexts causes unexpected interactions.
  • Creating trivial state classes for tiny variations can add unnecessary complexity.
Key Takeaway

Model each distinct behavior as a state class and let the context switch states to change behavior instead of piling conditionals into the context.

Definition & Analogy

Traffic light / MediaPlayer metaphor

A traffic light behaves differently when it is Red, Yellow, or Green. Each state class contains logic for that state and can decide which state comes next.

Concrete example
MediaPlayer states implement play, pause, stop. The MediaPlayer context holds a PlayerState reference and delegates calls. When the PlayingState handles pause, it sets the context to PausedState.
Check your understanding
Name a class in your project that uses a mode flag and imagine turning that logic into state classes. What are the new state names?

screens.title: State pattern structure
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the roles in the State pattern clarifies how responsibilities are divided. The Context is the object whose behavior changes; it maintains a reference to a State interface and delegates state-specific requests. The State interface declares the operations that vary with state, for example play, pause, and stop in the MediaPlayer example. Concrete State classes implement that interface and encapsulate behavior and transition logic: when they handle a request they may change the context's current state by calling the context's setState method. This design keeps the context free of conditionals and places transition logic where it belongs. A concrete example: PlayingState prints a message when play is called, pauses transition to PausedState, and stop transitions to StoppedState. A misconception to avoid is coupling State implementations to external systems; state classes should focus on state behavior and call into the context when necessary, keeping side effects explicit and testable. Test each state independently and verify transitions by asserting the context's resulting state. State pattern structure means context delegates; state interface defines operations; concrete states implement behavior and manage transitions.. In practical terms, context, state interface, and concrete states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Pattern Structure
Context
MediaPlayer (example)

Holds a reference to the current state and delegates requests such as play, pause, stop to that state. It exposes setState so states can trigger transitions.

Why this helps
Context becomes simpler, with no branching on state values.
State Interface
PlayerState

Defines operations all concrete states must implement, like play(MediaPlayer), pause(MediaPlayer), stop(MediaPlayer). Keeps concrete states interchangeable.

Test tip
Mock the context when unit testing state behavior to verify transitions without full system setup.
Concrete States
PlayingState, PausedState, StoppedState

Implement concrete behavior. They may call context.setState(new OtherState()) to change behavior in response to events.

Pitfall
Avoid placing broad application logic in state classes; keep state classes focused on state-specific behavior and small transitions.

screens.title: MediaPlayer Java walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the MediaPlayer example in Java to see how the pieces fit. Start with a PlayerState interface declaring play, pause, and stop methods that accept a MediaPlayer context. Each concrete state implements these methods and, when appropriate, calls the context's setState with a new state instance to perform transitions. For example, PlayingState. pause sets the context to PausedState, while StoppedState. play sets it to PlayingState. The MediaPlayer context stores a PlayerState reference and delegates calls: when clickPlay is invoked, the context forwards the call to state. play(this). This removes conditional switches from MediaPlayer and places transition logic in concrete states. A common misconception is to store and mutate shared state objects between multiple MediaPlayer instances for efficiency; avoid this unless the state is immutable or properly synchronized. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › MediaPlayer Code
Code
// State interface
interface PlayerState {
void play(MediaPlayer player);
void pause(MediaPlayer player);
void stop(MediaPlayer player);
}
// Example: PlayingState
class PlayingState implements PlayerState {
public void play(MediaPlayer p){ System.out.println("Already playing."); }
public void pause(MediaPlayer p){ System.out.println("Pausing media."); p.setState(new PausedState()); }
public void stop(MediaPlayer p){ System.out.println("Stopping media."); p.setState(new StoppedState()); }
}
Runtime & Testing
Console trace (example)
Starting media from beginning. Media Player state changed to: PlayingState
Pausing media. Media Player state changed to: PausedState
Testing suggestion
Write a unit test that calls play on a MediaPlayer in StoppedState and asserts that the new state is PlayingState and that the correct message is produced or side effects occur.
Common misconception
Don't conflate state classes with strategy classes; states often manage transitions between each other instead of being stateless strategies.

screens.title: What is the Chain of Responsibility?
screens.narratorSegment: The Chain of Responsibility pattern gives multiple objects a chance to handle a request by forming a chain of handlers. The sender sends the request to the first handler, and each handler decides whether to handle the request or forward it to the next handler. This pattern decouples the sender from concrete receivers and lets you add or reorder handlers without changing client code. A classic example is a logging chain: a ConsoleLogger might handle info and above, a FileLogger handles debug and above, and an EmailLogger handles error and above. When a message is logged, each logger that is configured to handle that level writes the message and may forward it. Another common use is approval workflows: a Team Lead can approve small purchases, otherwise it passes to a Department Manager, then to a CEO. Be mindful of two pitfalls: ensure that requests are eventually handled or explicitly rejected, and avoid chains that become so long they harm performance or observability. Consider whether each handler should both handle and continue passing a request, or stop propagation after handling. What is the Chain of Responsibility? means chain of responsibility passes a request along a sequence of handlers until one handles it, decoupling sender and receiver.. In practical terms, decouple senders from receivers by passing requests along a chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Chain of Responsibility
Core Idea

Chain of Responsibility

Handlers are linked. Each handler either processes the request or delegates it to the next handler.

Example: Logging chain
ConsoleLogger handles INFO+, FileLogger handles DEBUG+, EmailLogger handles ERROR+. A log request flows along the chain and each capable logger writes the message.
Pitfall
Chains that do not handle a request should either reject it or provide a default handler to avoid silent failures.
Analogy

Customer support tiers

A support ticket first goes to Tier 1. If unresolved, it moves to Tier 2, then Tier 3. Each tier decides to resolve or escalate.

Design tip
Define clear responsibilities for each handler and document when handlers should pass requests onward to maintain observability.

screens.title: Chain pattern structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Chain of Responsibility comprises three main roles. The Handler interface declares methods to set the next handler and to process the request. Concrete Handlers implement this interface and decide whether to handle the request or forward it. The Client sends a request to the first handler in the chain. In a logging example, the abstract Logger stores a LogLevel and a reference to the nextLogger. Its logMessage method checks whether this handler should handle the incoming level and, if so, calls write. Then it forwards the request to nextLogger if present. Concrete handlers like ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, and EmailLogger implement write to perform their action. Build the chain by linking handlers and pass requests to the first handler. A crucial design decision is whether handlers should both write and forward, or write and stop. That choice affects whether multiple handlers may process a single request. Also design for graceful fallback when the end of the chain is reached: either reject, log, or provide a default handler. Chain pattern structure means handler interface defines processing; concrete handlers decide to handle or pass; client initiates a request at the chain start.. In practical terms, handler interface, concrete handlers, and client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Chain Structure
Handler Interface
abstract Logger

Declares setNextLogger and logMessage. Keeps a LogLevel and reference to the next handler in the chain.

Concrete Handlers
ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, EmailLogger

Each implements write() with handler-specific behavior. They decide based on level whether to write and may forward after writing.

Client
Chain builder & caller

Construct the chain by linking handlers and send requests to the first handler to start processing.

Design question
Should a handler stop propagation after handling? Decide based on whether multiple handlers should process the same request.
Operational tip
Ensure chains do not silently drop requests: include a default rejection or final logger to capture unhandled requests.

screens.title: Logger chain Java walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Now we examine the logger chain example in Java to see Chain of Responsibility in action. An abstract Logger holds a LogLevel and a reference to the next logger. Its logMessage method compares the incoming level with the logger's level and calls write if appropriate. After writing, it forwards the request to nextLogger if present, allowing multiple loggers to act on the same message. Concrete handlers implement write: ConsoleLogger prints to the console, FileLogger simulates a file write, and EmailLogger simulates sending an alert. The client constructs the chain by creating a ConsoleLogger for INFO, a FileLogger for DEBUG, and an EmailLogger for ERROR, and then links them in order. When a DEBUG message is logged, both ConsoleLogger and FileLogger write; when an ERROR is logged, all three write. A practical pitfall is forgetting to set the nextLogger, which truncates the chain, or misconfiguring levels so some messages never reach an intended handler. Test your chain by sending messages at different levels and asserting which handlers produced output. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Logger Chain
Code Snippet
abstract class Logger { protected LogLevel level; protected Logger nextLogger; public Logger(LogLevel level){ this.level = level; } public void setNextLogger(Logger next){ this.nextLogger = next; } public void logMessage(LogLevel lvl, String msg){ if(this.level.ordinal() <= lvl.ordinal()){ write(msg); } if(nextLogger != null){ nextLogger.logMessage(lvl, msg); } } protected abstract void write(String message); }
Runtime Example
Expected console output
Console Log: This is an information.
Console Log: This is a debug level information.\nFile Log: This is a debug level information.
Console Log: This is an error level information.\nFile Log: This is an error level information.\nEmail Alert: This is an error level information.
Debugging tip
If a handler never runs, verify its level ordinal and confirm it is linked into the chain with setNextLogger.

screens.title: Approval workflow: Chain of Responsibility exercise
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on exercise uses Chain of Responsibility to implement an approval workflow. The PurchaseRequest class contains amount, description, and status. An ApprovalHandler interface defines setNextHandler and processRequest. Concrete handlers implement logic: TeamLead approves requests under one thousand dollars, DepartmentManager approves from one thousand to five thousand, and the CEO approves above five thousand. The chain is built by linking TeamLead to DepartmentManager to CEO, then the client sends requests to the first handler. For each request, a handler either approves and sets the request status or prints a message and passes the request onward. When designing your implementation, ensure the handler forwards the request only when it cannot approve and that each handler prints a clear message indicating approval or forwarding. A frequent mistake is mis-specified thresholds that cause requests to be rejected or approved at the wrong level; write tests for boundary amounts. After implementing, run several requests across thresholds and verify the status field matches the approving role. What logging would help you diagnose an unexpected approval path? In practical terms, model purchase approvals using teamlead → departmentmanager → ceo. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: When to use State vs Chain of Responsibility
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between State and Chain of Responsibility depends on the design problem you face. Use State when the central object has behavior that varies by internal mode and you want to move branching logic into state classes; this improves cohesion for state-specific behavior and simplifies the context. Use Chain of Responsibility when you need flexible processing pipelines where multiple independent handlers may inspect or act on a request and you want to decouple the sender from the receivers. Structurally, State centers on context plus interchangeable state objects; Chain centers on a linked sequence of handlers. A common trade-off is complexity: State increases the number of classes and moves transitions into those classes, which is great when states encapsulate meaningful behavior, but can be overkill for trivial flags. Chain gives flexible ordering and dynamic configuration, but chains that grow too long can be harder to debug and may impact performance. Consider testability: states are easy to unit test in isolation, whereas chains benefit from integration tests that verify propagation and termination. State Pattern
Best for mode-driven behavior

Chain Pattern
Best for processing pipelines
  • Handlers can be added, removed, or reordered.
  • Decouples sender from receivers.

screens.title: Best practices and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: To use these patterns safely, adopt a few best practices. First, keep state classes focused and testable: write unit tests for each concrete state that exercise transitions and side effects. Avoid sharing mutable state instances across contexts; prefer per-context instances or immutable shared instances. Second, document transitions clearly so it's easy to see which state can switch to which other states. Third, for chains, ensure that every request is either handled or explicitly rejected; include a final handler or a default rejection to avoid silent drops. Fourth, choose whether handlers should both act and continue propagation or stop after handling. That decision affects observability and debugging. Fifth, log decisions at handler boundaries so you can trace why a request moved from one handler to the next. Common mistakes include excessive fragmentation into tiny state classes for trivial differences, or very long chains that are hard to reason about. Finally, when refactoring, prefer incremental changes: extract one state or handler at a time and add tests to ensure behavior remains stable. screens.title: Applying patterns in designs
screens.narratorSegment: Let's close the lesson with a practical application: refactoring a monolithic class with many conditionals. Start by identifying the longest conditional or switch statement tied to an internal mode or an ordered pipeline of checks. If the logic switches behavior based on a mode and has stateful transitions, extract a State interface and move each branch into a concrete state. If the logic represents independent processing steps that may be reordered or extended, model each step as a handler in a Chain of Responsibility. Use the following checklist when refactoring: write tests that capture current behavior; identify boundaries and responsibilities; extract the smallest safe unit into a state or handler; run tests and iterate. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore two behavioral patterns that tame conditional complexity. First, you will learn the State pattern, which models behavior variations by encapsulating each state into its own class so an object effectively changes its behavior as its internal state changes. You will see how a MediaPlayer can move between Playing, Paused, and Stopped without sprawling switch statements. Second, you will learn the Chain of Responsibility pattern, which lets a request travel through a sequence of handlers until one handles it, useful for logging levels, approval flows, or multi-stage processing. We will walk through Java examples for both patterns, point out common pitfalls such as mutable shared state or chains that never terminate, and practice a small approval workflow. By the end you will know how to choose between encapsulating state transitions or delegating handling in a chain, how to implement each pattern in Java, and where each pattern improves maintainability. Think about how these patterns reduce coupling and make behavior easier to extend.

These learning objectives frame the skills you'll practice. First, you'll explain how the State pattern enables an object to alter its behavior as its internal state changes. That means you will be able to describe how a context delegates to state objects and why this keeps conditional logic out of the context. Second, you will implement the State pattern in Java: write a state interface, concrete state classes, and a context such as a MediaPlayer that switches states. You will practice a concrete example where play, pause, and stop are delegated to state objects. Third, you will understand the Chain of Responsibility pattern, how it decouples senders from receivers and how a request flows along handlers. Fourth, you will apply Chain of Responsibility to build flexible pipelines like logging or approval flows where each handler decides to handle or pass the request. Each objective includes a short cognitive goal and a practical reason why it matters, so you can connect the concept to real design choices.

These additional objectives focus on decision-making and evaluation. You will identify benefits and drawbacks of each pattern so you can choose the right tool for a design problem. For the State pattern you will learn common pitfalls such as sharing mutable state objects across contexts and creating too many trivial state classes. For the Chain of Responsibility you will learn to avoid chains that never handle a request or become excessively long, and how to ensure requests are handled or explicitly rejected. You will also practice a hands-on activity: build an approval workflow that routes purchase requests to Team Lead, Department Manager, and CEO based on amount thresholds. Finally, you will compare the patterns and practice refactoring a conditional-laden context into one or both patterns, assessing trade-offs in clarity, extensibility, and runtime overhead.

The State pattern is a behavioral design pattern that lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes. In plain terms, instead of a single class filled with if-else or switch blocks checking a state variable, you model each distinct state as a class that implements a common state interface. The original object, called the context, holds a reference to the current state and delegates state-specific operations to it. A concrete example from the source is a MediaPlayer: Playing, Paused, and Stopped are separate classes implementing play, pause, and stop methods. When the context delegates a call to its current state, the result depends on that state’s implementation. This makes adding a new state a matter of adding a new class rather than modifying a large conditional. A common misconception is to think you should share a single mutable state instance between contexts to save objects. That often leads to subtle bugs: prefer distinct state instances or manage shared instances carefully. In short, State trades conditional complexity for small, focused classes and clearer transition logic. Consider: what state transitions in your app are causing long conditional chains?

Understanding the roles in the State pattern clarifies how responsibilities are divided. The Context is the object whose behavior changes; it maintains a reference to a State interface and delegates state-specific requests. The State interface declares the operations that vary with state, for example play, pause, and stop in the MediaPlayer example. Concrete State classes implement that interface and encapsulate behavior and transition logic: when they handle a request they may change the context's current state by calling the context's setState method. This design keeps the context free of conditionals and places transition logic where it belongs. A concrete example: PlayingState prints a message when play is called, pauses transition to PausedState, and stop transitions to StoppedState. A misconception to avoid is coupling State implementations to external systems; state classes should focus on state behavior and call into the context when necessary, keeping side effects explicit and testable. Test each state independently and verify transitions by asserting the context's resulting state. In practical terms, context, state interface, and concrete states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the MediaPlayer example in Java to see how the pieces fit. Start with a PlayerState interface declaring play, pause, and stop methods that accept a MediaPlayer context. Each concrete state implements these methods and, when appropriate, calls the context's setState with a new state instance to perform transitions. For example, PlayingState. pause sets the context to PausedState, while StoppedState. play sets it to PlayingState. The MediaPlayer context stores a PlayerState reference and delegates calls: when clickPlay is invoked, the context forwards the call to state. play(this). This removes conditional switches from MediaPlayer and places transition logic in concrete states. A common misconception is to store and mutate shared state objects between multiple MediaPlayer instances for efficiency; avoid this unless the state is immutable or properly synchronized. When testing, instantiate each concrete state and verify its responses given a mock or simple MediaPlayer context. Finally, observe runtime output in the example: transitions print messages and the context's state class name, illustrating how behavior emerges from the current state object. The Chain of Responsibility pattern gives multiple objects a chance to handle a request by forming a chain of handlers. The sender sends the request to the first handler, and each handler decides whether to handle the request or forward it to the next handler. This pattern decouples the sender from concrete receivers and lets you add or reorder handlers without changing client code. A classic example is a logging chain: a ConsoleLogger might handle info and above, a FileLogger handles debug and above, and an EmailLogger handles error and above. When a message is logged, each logger that is configured to handle that level writes the message and may forward it. Another common use is approval workflows: a Team Lead can approve small purchases, otherwise it passes to a Department Manager, then to a CEO. Be mindful of two pitfalls: ensure that requests are eventually handled or explicitly rejected, and avoid chains that become so long they harm performance or observability. Consider whether each handler should both handle and continue passing a request, or stop propagation after handling. Concrete Handlers implement this interface and decide whether to handle the request or forward it. The Client sends a request to the first handler in the chain. In a logging example, the abstract Logger stores a LogLevel and a reference to the nextLogger. Its logMessage method checks whether this handler should handle the incoming level and, if so, calls write. Then it forwards the request to nextLogger if present. Concrete handlers like ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, and EmailLogger implement write to perform their action. Build the chain by linking handlers and pass requests to the first handler. A crucial design decision is whether handlers should both write and forward, or write and stop. That choice affects whether multiple handlers may process a single request. Also design for graceful fallback when the end of the chain is reached: either reject, log, or provide a default handler. Here are three compact reminders to carry forward for the State pattern. First, the State pattern allows an object to alter its behavior as its internal state changes by delegating state-specific behavior to separate state classes. Second, the Context is the object whose behavior changes; it holds a reference to the current state and delegates requests. Third, the State interface defines the contract for concrete states, ensuring interchangeability and keeping the context independent of specific implementations. Use these three ideas when you see large conditionals tied to an object's mode: model states explicitly, test them independently, and manage transitions inside states to keep the context clean.
